title: Circular and Projectile Motion
learning_goal: Describe and analyze acceleration in uniform circular motion and horizontal projectile motion.

stages.title: 1. Two kinds of accelerated motion
stages.content: An object can accelerate even when its speed is constant if its direction changes. In uniform circular motion, velocity continuously changes direction toward the center. In projectile motion, horizontal and vertical motions occur at the same time.

stages.title: 2. Uniform circular motion
stages.content: For an object moving in a circle at constant speed, centripetal acceleration points toward the center of the circle. Its magnitude is a = v²/r.

stages.title: 3. Worked example: circular motion
stages.content: A 2 kg object moves at 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m. The centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = 6²/3 = 12 m/s².

stages.title: 4. Horizontal projectile motion
stages.content: For a horizontally launched object, horizontal velocity remains constant if air resistance is ignored, while gravity causes vertical acceleration downward at about 9.8 m/s².

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A ball moves at 8 m/s around a circular path of radius 4 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
stages.hint: Use a = v²/r. Square the speed before dividing by the radius.
stages.alternate_explanation: Think of the object as constantly turning. The faster it moves or the tighter the circle, the greater the inward acceleration.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, identify the direction of centripetal acceleration, calculate a = v²/r, separate horizontal and vertical projectile motion, and explain how gravity affects the vertical component.

concept_cards.title: Constant speed can still mean acceleration
concept_cards.content: Velocity includes direction. Around a circle, the velocity arrow continually turns even if speed stays fixed. For uniform circular motion, velocity is tangent to the path and acceleration points toward the center.

concept_cards.title: Why the circular acceleration is inward
concept_cards.content: Over a short interval, the difference between successive velocity vectors points inward. The net force produces this inward acceleration. Depending on the situation, tension, friction, gravity, or a normal force can supply the net inward force. There is no separate extra centripetal force.

concept_cards.title: The size of centripetal acceleration
concept_cards.content: Use a_c = v²/r. Doubling speed at fixed radius makes acceleration four times as large. Doubling radius at fixed speed halves the acceleration. If the inward interaction disappears, the object initially moves along the tangent, not radially outward.

concept_cards.title: Projectile motion combines independent components
concept_cards.content: Ignoring air resistance near Earth, horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is downward, approximately 9.8 m/s². A horizontally launched projectile starts with zero vertical velocity, not zero vertical acceleration. Its horizontal velocity stays constant while downward speed increases.

concept_cards.title: Same fall time under the same conditions
concept_cards.content: An object dropped from rest and one launched horizontally from the same height at the same instant reach level ground together if air resistance is negligible. Both begin with zero vertical velocity and undergo the same gravitational acceleration. Horizontal speed affects range, not fall time, under these conditions.

worked_examples.prompt: An object moves at constant speed 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m. Find the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration.

visual.label: Velocity is tangent to the circle; acceleration points inward.

hint_steps: Speed can stay constant while velocity changes direction.
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: The object continually turns. Acceleration changes the direction of velocity even when its magnitude stays constant. A tighter circle or a higher speed requires a larger inward acceleration.
alternate_explanation_steps: Use a_c = (6 m/s)² ÷ (3 m).
This gives 12 m/s², directed toward the center.
Centripetal describes the direction of net acceleration. It is not an additional kind of force.

conceptual_questions.prompt: A car turns at constant speed. Explain why it accelerates even though its speed does not change.
expected_ideas: Velocity includes direction, and the direction changes while turning.
For uniform circular motion, acceleration points toward the center.
misconceptions: Acceleration requires a change in speed.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: Does the velocity arrow keep the same direction around the circle?

conceptual_questions.prompt: A ball moves in a horizontal circle on a string. Viewed from above, what direction does it initially travel if the string breaks? Explain.
expected_ideas: The ball initially travels along the tangent in its instantaneous velocity direction.
The string no longer supplies the inward force needed to keep turning.
misconceptions: The ball initially shoots radially away from the center.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: Which direction was the velocity pointing immediately before the break?

conceptual_questions.prompt: One ball is dropped and another is launched horizontally from the same height at the same instant. With negligible air resistance, compare their fall times and explain.
expected_ideas: Both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same downward acceleration.
They reach the same level ground together; horizontal motion does not change vertical fall time in this model.
misconceptions: The horizontally launched ball stays in the air longer solely because it moves horizontally.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What differs between their vertical initial conditions?

conceptual_questions.prompt: For a projectile launched horizontally, does increasing downward speed mean its horizontal speed must decrease? Explain, ignoring air resistance.
expected_ideas: Gravity provides vertical acceleration and no horizontal acceleration.
Horizontal speed stays constant while vertical speed increases; total speed increases.
misconceptions: Horizontal motion is used up to create vertical motion.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What horizontal force acts after launch in this ideal model?
